subject: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
I recently modified a model to pre-compute a model-matrix rather than generate it on the fly and pass the model matrix in as data.  What used to be a mess of Stan
functions turns into X * b and I get a nice speed-up even with X being ~50000x200... I did have some issues getting this running (like stan_rdump choking on the 'gsub'
expression but if you remove the gsub commands it works fine).  The model matrix is pretty sparse (>75% 0's) but I understand at the moment there is no sparse data type
in Stan.  I noticed some pointers under the sparse data section of the manual, but I don't see an obvious way of making them apply to the situation where your ultimate
goal is making X * b go fast. 

One way of solving it would be to keep the non-zero entries of each row of X, a vector of which entries are non-zero, and code the sparse multiplication by hand.  Are
there any efficiency reasons to make this a function defined in Stan's function block versus coding it in C++ and adding it to Stan's functions?

My question is if I'm missing something here---is there a better way of achieving this?  I'm running a lot of these models and when they were each taking under a day
each it was fine but it seems worth it to do some more optimization now.  I know that X * b could be recoded to do more indexing via functions in the Stan model but
coding new indexing methods all the time in Stan is more error-prone than coding/testing them in R.

Thanks for any suggestions.

Krzysztof

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
It is probably hard to get much more speed with just Stan code. If your observations are exchangeable, then maybe it is possible to reorder the observations into groups that each have a common sparseness pattern. If you only pass in the dense columns for each group, you could subset the coefficient vector accordingly so that it is conformable for multiplication with that group's design matrix. Then you are just doing a few matrix-vector multiplications.

Better would be to contribute something in C++. We don't have many sparse matrix operations internally, but we have talked about it. You would probably gain more from utilizing the fact that the Jacobian matrix of eta = X * beta is X than you would from the sparseness.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
I'm afraid we don't have sparseness yet. It's been
part of our recent grant proposals, so if we get one
of those, we'll be on the hook to do it over the
next couple of years. It requires specifying I/O,
plumbing through the language, and plumbing through
all the interfaces. Then we actually have to provide
some useful sparse matrix functions, which means a whole
lot more integration with the Eigen sparse matrix lib.
Not fundamentally hard, just a long slog.

If you don't provide customized gradients, there should
be no difference between writing a function in C++ and writing
a function in Stan --- they'll get compiled to the same
underlying C++ in the end.

If you do come up with handy Stan functions, I'm sure
others would appreciate seeing what they are so they could
follow (including me for the manual!).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
On Wednesday, February 18, 2015 at 8:45:13 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
If your likelihood is just a lot of independent Gaussians, you could do the completing the square trick to express it as the deviation from the least squares values that can be precomputed.

That's a good point, but no such luck. It's the models for phi[i]/p[i]/alpha[i]/rho[i] for this mess (a survival model): 

data {
  int n_rows;
  int n_censored;
  int n_ambiguous_individuals;

  int n_unambiguous_rows;
  int n_ambiguous_rows;
  int n_individuals;
  int ambiguous_rows[n_ambiguous_individuals,2];
  int unambiguous_rows[n_unambiguous_rows];

  vector[n_rows] interval;
  int season[n_rows];
  int cjs_classification[n_rows];
}

transformed data {
  int ambig_row_calc_buffer;
  int m;

  ambig_row_calc_buffer <- 0;
  for ( i in 1:n_ambiguous_individuals ) {
    m <- ambiguous_rows[i,2] - ambiguous_rows[i,1] + 1;
    if ( m > ambig_row_calc_buffer ) {
      ambig_row_calc_buffer <- m;
    }
  }
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> phi_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> p_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> rho_seasonal[4];
}

model {
  real row_lp[n_rows];
  int k;
  int start_row;
  int stop_row;
  real A[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real A_star[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real B[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real B_star[ambig_row_calc_buffer];

  vector[n_rows] phi;
  vector[n_rows] p;
  vector[n_rows] alpha;
  vector[n_rows] rho;

  for ( i in 1:4 ) {
    phi_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,5);
    p_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,5);
    alpha_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,25);
    rho_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,25);
  }

  for ( i in 1:n_rows ) {
    phi[i] <- pow(phi_seasonal[season[i]],interval[i]*(4/365.25));
    p[i] <- p_seasonal[season[i]];
    alpha[i] <- alpha_seasonal[season[i]];
    rho[i] <- rho_seasonal[season[i]];
  }                                                                                            
  for ( i in 1:n_unambiguous_rows ) {
    k <- unambiguous_rows[i];
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 0) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated.");
      row_lp[k] <- 0.0;
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 1) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k])*p[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 2) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k])*(1-p[k]));
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 3) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*rho[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 4) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*rho[k]*alpha[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 5) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k]));
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 6) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated here.");
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 7) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated.");
      row_lp[k] <- 0.0;
    }
    increment_log_prob(row_lp[k]);
  }

  for ( i in 1:(n_ambiguous_individuals)) {
    for ( j in 1:ambig_row_calc_buffer ) {
      A[j] <- 0.0;
      B[j] <- 0.0;
      A_star[j] <- 0.0;
      B_star[j] <- 0.0;
    }
    start_row <- ambiguous_rows[i,1];
    stop_row <- ambiguous_rows[i,2];
    for ( j in start_row:stop_row ) {
      k <- j - start_row + 1;
      if (cjs_classification[j] != 6) {
        print("STOP, row ", j, " should not be evaluated here.");
      }
      if (j == start_row) {
        A[k] <- 1.0;
        A_star[k] <- 1.0;
      } else {
        A[k] <- phi[j-1]*(1-p[j-1]);
      }
      B[k] <- (1-phi[j]);

      A_star[k] <- A_star[k] * A[k];
      B_star[k] <- A_star[k] * B[k];

    }
    increment_log_prob(log(sum(B_star)));
  }


}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
Krzysztof brought up a number of points that
I'm going to try to collect into one response.
Thanks, Krzysztof!

This would probably be better as an issue we can
update and comment on.
> So it seems like there's room for a limited contribution on the C++ side just to get the sparse version of X*b coded, where X must be data and b's are parameters, with the associated gradients.

This would break our general rule of implementing all
of our functions for arbitrary var/double inputs.
(The only violation of which is for the ODE solver, which
isn't a function so much as a special statement with its
own grammar and error handling/messages.)
If it's implemented, it should allow X to be double
or agrad::var, and b should be able to be double
or agrad::var.
> I can see including sparse operations everywhere is going to be a long slong. Is there room here for me to do something very limited

Absolutely. But it needs to be a step toward where we
want to go in the long run. We want to be able to maintain
backward compatibility as we go.

> --I'm thinking:
>
> a) Stan function to turn a matrix X into a sparse representation

Why would you start with a dense matrix and turn it
into a sparse matrix? Would you test == 0?
> (one function per part of the sparse matrix representation since Stan has no ragged data structure).

Sparse and ragged are two different concepts. A ragged matrix
would have rows of different sizes, but they'd all be dense and
indexed 1 to N[row], where N[row] is the size of the row.
> b) Stan function to do a sparse X*b, using the output from a)
What were you thinking in terms of data structure for X?

>
> then
>
> c) C++ level function to do sparse X*b, and also provide the gradient calculation---only with X being data and b being parameters.
See above.
> I seem to remember the slow part of the gradients is evaluating a tree of partial derivatives---

My recollection from the last time profiling this is that
building the expression graph (it's not necessary a tree,
but it will be acyclic and directed) took about 20--30% of
the time and propagating derivatives took about 70--80% of
the time.

> would having this C++ level function collapse
> the part of the tree related to X*b into just one node?
That's always a win.

> That would be a reasonable speedup for not too much effort (on my part---I get that you
> guys have a schedule for the bigger project of including sparse calculations everywhere).

We don't really have a schedule, just a list of
roughly prioritized feature requests.
Everyone pretty much works on what they want.

> So doing this naively and (obviously) without gradients is a small to moderate win in terms of speed (test script attached). You do get memory savings as a bonus which might make it worth the effort.
Memory savings are very good.

> My implementation is naive so there are probably ways to make it go faster (like looking up what the sparse matrix multiplication algorithm is supposed to be for matrix * vector in this storage format)...
Which storage format?

> the attached function uses the dgCMatrix class from R to create the sparse matrix b/c this class can be mapped from R to Eigen easily using Rcpp (the RcppEigen introduction/vignette has some examples) so maybe it'll be handy for doing a C++ version.

Is the dgCMatrix class in R only going to be used
in RStan? We don't want any dependencies from
the base Stan C++ code to R because the license (GPL)
is too restrictive (Stan is BSD).

Here's the Stan function; I have no idea what it's supposed
to do. I'm a bit too tired to work it out from first
principles. It would be a huge help if you could doc it
describing what the arguments represent.

In general, functions should test that their inputs are
valid unless you can control how it's called yourself.
But that can always be added later

-------------
vector sparse_multiply(int N, int K, int[] q, int[] i, vector x, vector b) {
vector[N] y;
int m;
int ii;
m <- 1;
for (j in 1:N) y[j] <- 0.0;
for (j in 1:K) {
if (q[j] > 0) {
for (k in 1:(q[j])) {
ii <- i[m] + 1;
y[ii] <- y[ii] + x[m] * b[j];
m <- m + 1;
}
}
}
return y;
}
-------------

It looks like your coding of i is off by one if you have to
do this:

ii <- i[m] + 1;

Why not just pass in the proper offsets?

Also, I'd recommend against using i as the name of an integer
array since it's so conventionally associated with a single int.
Andrew and Jennifer Hill used the opposite convention, where ii
was an array of ints and i was an int.

Replace

for (j in 1:N) y[j] <- 0.0;

with y <- rep_vector(0,N);

You should drop the conditional

if (q[j] > 0) {
for (k in 1:(q[j])) {

Stan isn't R --- the A:B syntax is always rising.
so if q[j] == 0, then

for (k in 1:q[j])

will not execute its body and the test is redundant.
Branching can be a real slowdown (though unlikely to be
problematic here).

Declare local variables as close as possible to where
you use them. For example, the declaration of ii should
be inside the loop

for (k in 1:(q[j])) {

You can violate that rule for allocating containers that
you reuse.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
Quick answers below, I'll address the requests when I have time to get back to this....
my main question now is: do you have a preferred sparse storage format I should go with?
Eigen seems to support compressed row and compressed column, and I think even a
Stan function should follow what C++ will ultimately use.

Krzysztof

On Thursday, February 19, 2015 at 6:03:14 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Krzysztof brought up a number of points that
I'm going to try to collect into one response.
Thanks, Krzysztof!

This would probably be better as an issue we can
update and comment on.
Ok, I'll make an issue next time I poke this along.

> So it seems like there's room for a limited contribution on the C++ side just to get the sparse version of X*b coded, where X must be data and b's are parameters, with the associated gradients.

This would break our general rule of implementing all
of our functions for arbitrary var/double inputs.  
(The only violation of which is for the ODE solver, which
isn't a function so much as a special statement with its
own grammar and error handling/messages.)
If it's implemented, it should allow X to be double
or agrad::var, and b should be able to be double
or agrad::var.
I see how it would be confusing, I was thinking it might be a straightforward way for me to touch Stan C++ code but just doing the combinations you are describing doesn't seem bad.

> I can see including sparse operations everywhere is going to be a long slong.  Is there room here for me to do something very limited

Absolutely.  But it needs to be a step toward where we
want to go in the long run.  We want to be able to maintain
backward compatibility as we go.

> --I'm thinking:
>
> a) Stan function to turn a matrix X into a sparse representation

Why would you start with a dense matrix and turn it
into a sparse matrix?  Would you test == 0?
Yeah, the thought was to do it this way so you could have it both ways for testing, but I ended up skipping this step---it's just easier to marshall tests from the R side.

> (one function per part of the sparse matrix representation since Stan has no ragged data structure).

Sparse and ragged are two different concepts.  A ragged matrix
would have rows of different sizes, but they'd all be dense and
indexed 1 to N[row], where N[row] is the size of the row.

To me most sparse matrix formats look like they're implementing the matrix as a ragged array and doing extra to keep the indexes but having done this example I can see there's a little more finesse to it.

> b) Stan function to do a sparse X*b, using the output from a)

What were you thinking in terms of data structure for X?
Whatever Eigen does to make future reuse easier---either compressed column or compressed row storage (http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialSparse.html)

>
> then
>
> c) C++ level function to do sparse X*b, and also provide the gradient calculation---only with X being data and b being parameters.  

See above.

> I seem to remember the slow part of the gradients is evaluating a tree of partial derivatives---

My recollection from the last time profiling this is that
building the expression graph (it's not necessary a tree,
but it will be acyclic and directed) took about 20--30% of
the time and propagating derivatives took about 70--80% of
the time.

> would having this C++ level function collapse
> the part of the tree related to X*b into just one node?  

That's always a win.
Ok, thanks for confirming that that's part of the goal here.

> That would be a reasonable speedup for not too much effort (on my part---I get that you
> guys have a schedule for the bigger project of including sparse calculations everywhere).  


We don't really have a schedule, just a list of
roughly prioritized feature requests.  
Everyone pretty much works on what they want.

> So doing this naively and (obviously) without gradients is a small to moderate win in terms of speed (test script attached).  You do get memory savings as a bonus which might make it worth the effort.  

Memory savings are very good.
They're just not what I need at the moment, but easy even with the Stan function.

> My implementation is naive so there are probably ways to make it go faster (like looking up what the sparse matrix multiplication algorithm is supposed to be for matrix * vector in this storage format)...

Which storage format?
compressed column, maybe a little idiosyncratic since I lifted the description from R's help file.  Would it be better to go with Eigen's CCS specifically?

> the attached function uses the dgCMatrix class from R to create the sparse matrix b/c this class can be mapped from R to Eigen easily using Rcpp (the RcppEigen introduction/vignette has some examples) so maybe it'll be handy for doing a C++ version.


Is the dgCMatrix class in R only going to be used
in RStan?  We don't want any dependencies from
the base Stan C++ code to R because the license (GPL)
is too restrictive (Stan is BSD).
It's just (a version of) CCS.  Documented in ?'dgCMatrix-class'.  I'll redo based on whatever storage format gets chosen.

Here's the Stan function;  I have no idea what it's supposed
to do.  I'm a bit too tired to work it out from first
principles.   It would be a huge help if you could doc it
describing what the arguments represent.

Yep, once I settle on a storage format and go through this again I'll do a
little doc.

In general, functions should test that their inputs are
valid unless you can control how it's called yourself.
But that can always be added later

-------------
  vector sparse_multiply(int N, int K, int[] q, int[] i, vector x, vector b) {
    vector[N] y;
    int m;
    int ii;
    m <- 1;
    for (j in 1:N) y[j] <- 0.0;
    for (j in 1:K) {
      if (q[j] > 0) {
        for (k in 1:(q[j])) {
          ii <- i[m] + 1;
          y[ii] <- y[ii] + x[m] * b[j];
          m <- m + 1;
        }
      }
    }
    return y;
  }
-------------

It looks like your coding of i is off by one if you have to
do this:

          ii <- i[m] + 1;

Why not just pass in the proper offsets?

It's a note-to-self that the original indexing is 0-based, not 1-based.  The 'dgCMatrix' class holds the data in R but the methods
for it drop to C (C++?) code, like most of R's more efficient functions (so indexing from zero makes sense there).

Also, I'd recommend against using i as the name of an integer
array since it's so conventionally associated with a single int.
Andrew and Jennifer Hill used the opposite convention, where ii
was an array of ints and i was an int.

Replace

  for (j in 1:N) y[j] <- 0.0;

with y <- rep_vector(0,N);

You should drop the conditional

      if (q[j] > 0) {
        for (k in 1:(q[j])) {

Stan isn't R --- the A:B syntax is always rising.
so if q[j] == 0, then 

   for (k in 1:q[j])

will not execute its body and the test is redundant.
Branching can be a real slowdown (though unlikely to be
problematic here).

Declare local variables as close as possible to where
you use them.  For example, the declaration of ii should
be inside the loop

  for (k in 1:(q[j])) {

You can violate that rule for allocating containers that
you reuse.

OK, thanks for the hints, I'll do the changes when I post something more proper.
 

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
parts:
Thanks for the Eigen tutorial link. That's very helpful.
I'm not surprised they didn't literally use a ragged
array structure --- in fact they implemented a ragged-like
structure the way I suggested in the v2.6 manual chapter
(and was previously buried in the LDA model description).

We'd eventually want to use Eigen. We go with the
column major default for dense matrices now. It looks
like they default to compressed column, which makes sense
for consistency, so I'd just go with that. It does
make a difference in terms of how many other indices you
need to store, but neither dominates on all sparse matrices.

If you just implement a fully templated function, it'll
deal with all instantiations --- that's what the Stan functions
get compiled to. Then you can specialize for the cases you
really care about and build specialized derivatives.

At the other extreme are our density functions, which use
a lot of template magic to vectorize, drop constant terms,
and work for first and higher order autodiff. Everything
we do now needs to either take the templated route or also
implement forward mode. We're about to knock that off so
that we can do MML, VB, EP, etc.

- Bob

P.S. It seems like Google group's compressing losing all
indentation in replies. Very annoying. Did we mess up
a setting somewhere perhaps?
